criteria.criterion: Avoids a universal rule and frames a decision
criteria.evidence: Separate sections 'Why not just delete it this week' and 'Why not leave it forever'; says the team lead is right that it's debt and the cautious people are also right; recommends 'a staged experiment with a rollback, not a delete.'

criteria.criterion: Requires the workaround record fields (owner, scope, side effects, detection, exit)
criteria.evidence: Covers side effects ('a brief DHCP gap every night'), detection ('Build a detector before changing anything'), an exit condition ('Roll out node by node... then delete the cron') and archaeology into the cron's origin. It never names an owner and doesn't treat these as a formal record the workaround must have.

criteria.criterion: Proposes bounded testing of removal with detection and rollback
criteria.evidence: 'Disable the cron on one network node... dhcp_agents_per_network is at least 2... staging first'; 'Set the rollback trigger up front... Rolling back is re-enabling the cron'; uses a mismatch detector as the baseline.

'It will get copied into new deployments and survive upgrades unexamined' and 'it hides any real regression' get close to the idea. It never says outright that the restart has become a load-bearing part of the system that other things may now depend on.

criteria.criterion: Applies the 'risk introduced vs risk removed' test
criteria.evidence: Weighs the risks of removal (tenant-facing lease failures) against the risks of keeping it (the nightly DHCP gap, masked regressions), but only implicitly. It never states the test that removal is safe only while the risk introduced is less than the risk removed.

critical_errors.error: recommends removing it across all nodes immediately without detection or rollback
critical_errors.evidence: Explicitly argues against deleting it this week; requires a detector, a one-node canary, a rollback trigger and a node-by-node rollout.

critical_errors.error: recommends keeping it indefinitely without owner or review
critical_errors.evidence: 'Why not leave it forever' section; the plan ends either in removal or in a targeted, monitored replacement.

summary: The response is strong and practical. It turns 'remove now vs never touch it' into a decision: archaeology into the cron's origin, a detector built first, a one-node canary with redundant DHCP agents, a rollback trigger set up front, then a staged rollout. It commits neither critical error. Three gaps: it never assigns an owner for the workaround, it only gestures at accidental architecture, and it weighs the two sets of risks without stating the explicit 'risk introduced < risk removed' test. It makes no book citations and invents no facts about the user's environment.
